topics.title: Present simple: be
topics.summary: Match am, is and are to the subject, then build statements, negatives and questions.
topics.guidance: Read the short rules and examples, then complete a 20-question session. Use feedback to explain each choice. Revisit the skill you missed before trying again.

rules.title: Present forms
rules.explanation: Use am with I, is with a singular subject, and are with you or a plural subject. Be describes identity, location or a state.
examples: The keys are on a hook.

rules.title: Negatives and questions
rules.explanation: Place not after be. For a standard yes/no question, put be before the subject. Do not add do or does.

rules.title: Contractions
rules.explanation: In everyday English, I am becomes I’m and they are becomes they’re. Full forms remain correct. In positive short answers, keep the full verb.

tips: Read the full context before choosing.
Check the explanation, including after a correct answer.
A passing practice session is useful feedback, not a language certificate.

topics.title: Present simple
topics.summary: Talk about regular activities and practise agreement, negatives, questions and base forms.
topics.guidance: Read the short rules and examples, then complete a 20-question session. Use feedback to explain each choice. Revisit the skill you missed before trying again.

rules.title: Habits and facts
rules.explanation: Use the present simple for routines and general facts. With I, you, we and they, use the base verb. Most singular third-person subjects add -s.

rules.title: Spelling
rules.explanation: Some verbs add -es. A consonant followed by y usually changes to -ies; a vowel followed by y keeps the y.

rules.title: Do and does
rules.explanation: Use do or does for questions, and do not or does not for negatives. The main verb then returns to its base form.
examples: We do not work on Sundays.

tips: Read the full context before choosing.

topics.title: Present continuous
topics.summary: Describe actions happening now with the right form of be and an -ing form.
topics.guidance: Read the short rules and examples, then complete a 20-question session. Use feedback to explain each choice. Revisit the skill you missed before trying again.

rules.title: Actions in progress
rules.explanation: Use am, is or are plus an -ing form for an activity in progress now. The form of be agrees with the subject.
examples: The dog is sleeping by the fire.

rules.title: Building the verb
rules.explanation: Many verbs add -ing. Usually remove a final silent e; some short verbs double their last consonant. Learn spelling with the verb.

rules.title: Questions and negatives
rules.explanation: Move be before the subject in a question. Put not after be in a negative. Keep the -ing form in both.
examples: I am not using the lift.

tips: Read the full context before choosing.
Check the explanation, including after a correct answer.
A passing practice session is useful feedback, not a language certificate.

topics.title: Past simple
topics.summary: Use regular and irregular past forms and keep the base verb after did.
topics.guidance: Read the short rules and examples, then complete a 20-question session. Use feedback to explain each choice. Revisit the skill you missed before trying again.

rules.title: Completed past events
rules.explanation: Use the past simple for events at a finished past time. Regular forms often end in -ed; irregular forms must be learned.
examples: We booked a room last week.
The visitor spoke to the guide.

rules.title: Questions and negatives
rules.explanation: Did and did not carry the past tense. The main verb is the base form, even when its affirmative past is irregular.
examples: They did not bring a camera.

rules.title: Spelling and unchanged forms
rules.explanation: Some verbs change spelling; others keep the same written form. Read has the same spelling in the present and past but different pronunciation.

tips: Read the full context before choosing.
Check the explanation, including after a correct answer.
A passing practice session is useful feedback, not a language certificate.

topics.title: Articles: a, an and the
topics.summary: Choose an indefinite, definite or zero article using sound and context.
topics.guidance: Read the short rules and examples, then complete a 20-question session. Use feedback to explain each choice. Revisit the skill you missed before trying again.

rules.title: One nonspecific item
rules.explanation: Use a or an before a singular countable noun that is not yet identified. Choose by the next sound: an before a vowel sound and a before a consonant sound.

rules.title: An identified item
rules.explanation: Use the when the listener can identify the item, including a second mention. The also works with identified plural nouns.
examples: I found a ring. The ring was silver.

rules.title: General plural nouns
rules.explanation: Usually omit the article before a plural noun when referring to its whole class. In these exercises, — means no article.

tips: Read the full context before choosing.
Check the explanation, including after a correct answer.
A passing practice session is useful feedback, not a language certificate.

topics.title: Pronouns and possession
topics.summary: Distinguish subjects, objects, possessive determiners and possessive pronouns.
topics.guidance: Read the short rules and examples, then complete a 20-question session. Use feedback to explain each choice. Revisit the skill you missed before trying again.

rules.title: Subject and object
rules.explanation: Use I, he, she, we or they as subjects. Use me, him, her, us or them as objects. You and it keep the same form.

rules.title: Before a noun
rules.explanation: Use my, your, his, her, its, our or their directly before a noun. These determiners identify the owner.

rules.title: Replacing a noun phrase
rules.explanation: Mine, yours, his, hers, ours and theirs stand on their own. Do not add an apostrophe. His works both before a noun and on its own.

tips: Read the full context before choosing.
Check the explanation, including after a correct answer.
A passing practice session is useful feedback, not a language certificate.

topics.title: Prepositions of time
topics.summary: Practise at, on, in and no preposition with unambiguous time expressions.
topics.guidance: Read the short rules and examples, then complete a 20-question session. Use feedback to explain each choice. Revisit the skill you missed before trying again.

rules.title: At
rules.explanation: Use at with clock times and expressions such as noon, midnight and dawn.

rules.title: On and in
rules.explanation: Use on with days and dates, including a named day plus a part of that day. Use in with months and with the morning, afternoon or evening.

rules.title: No preposition
rules.explanation: Usually omit a time preposition before next, last, this or every, and before today, tomorrow and yesterday. Here, — means leave the gap empty.

tips: Read the full context before choosing.

topics.title: Comparatives and superlatives
topics.summary: Compare two things, identify an extreme in a group, and express equality.
topics.guidance: Read the short rules and examples, then complete a 20-question session. Use feedback to explain each choice. Revisit the skill you missed before trying again.

rules.title: Comparing two
rules.explanation: Many short adjectives add -er; longer adjectives often use more. Introduce the second item with than. Avoid adding more to an -er comparative.
examples: This route is shorter than that one.
The new seat is more comfortable.

rules.title: Comparing a group
rules.explanation: Use the plus a superlative: often -est or most plus the adjective. Good becomes better/best; bad becomes worse/worst.

rules.title: Equal degree
rules.explanation: Use as plus the base adjective plus as for equality. Spelling may change in comparative and superlative forms.
examples: The two boxes are as heavy as each other.

tips: Read the full context before choosing.
Check the explanation, including after a correct answer.
A passing practice session is useful feedback, not a language certificate.
